title: Searching for a Place
subtitle: Work, Affection and the Search for Belonging · 1869–1881
intro: A home, a livelihood, a relationship, a purpose. Each gives us a way into Vincent’s early life.
wallText: Follow the places and people that shaped these years. Letters preserve particular moments. Family recollections and later research offer further accounts, with questions that remain open.
imageCaption: Vincent van Gogh, aged nineteen · The Hague, January 1873
imageCredit: Photograph: J. M. W. de Louw · Public domain

timeline.title: The Art Trade
timeline.body: Work at Goupil & Cie brought Vincent into the world of paintings and prints before he became an artist.

timeline.title: Teaching & Faith
timeline.body: Teaching, religious work and study offered other possible ways to serve and to belong.

timeline.title: The Borinage
timeline.body: Life among miners deepened his concern for working people. His religious ambitions did not become a lasting vocation.

timeline.title: Learning to Draw
timeline.body: He turned increasingly to drawing and to the possibility of a life in art. Continue to the Early Works in Hall 01, then follow the route into Hall 02.

chapters.title: A New Home
chapters.subtitle: London, 1873
chapters.kicker: A YOUNG MAN, NOT YET A PAINTER
chapters.imageCaption: Vincent van Gogh, aged nineteen. Photograph by J. M. W. de Louw, The Hague, January 1873. Taken before his move to London.
chapters.imageCredit: Original photographic portrait · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain
paragraphs: In May 1873, twenty-year-old Vincent van Gogh arrived in London to work for the art dealer Goupil & Cie. By August, he had moved into lodgings at 87 Hackford Road.

At Hackford Road, Vincent boarded with the widowed Sarah Ursula Loyer and her daughter, Eugénie. The household also accommodated a small school for boys. For Mrs Loyer, teaching and letting rooms were ways of earning a living.

On 13 September 1873, Vincent described his new room to Theo. He was glad to have left behind the sloping beams and blue wallpaper with a green border of his previous lodgings. He found the household lively and wished his brother could see it.
The same letter moves easily from domestic news to an outing on the Thames and an exhibition of Belgian paintings. Home, companionship and pictures belonged to the same conversation.

quote.text: Oh! Old man, I so want that you come here to see my new lodgings
quote.attribution: Vincent to Theo · London, 13 September 1873 · Letter 13

chapters.prompt: Look beyond the famous name. What would you want to tell someone about your first home in a new city?
chapters.evidence: The portrait was taken in January 1873, before London. The letter documents his new room and the boys’ school. The house photograph shown here was taken on 17 May 2016, not in 1873. The letter excerpt is a typeset quotation from WebExhibits, not a manuscript image; its wording differs from the modern scholarly translation.
chapters.focus: Where did he live, and who shared the household?

chapters.title: A Life He Enjoyed
chapters.focus: What made everyday life in London rewarding?
chapters.subtitle: Art, Nature and Everyday Pleasure — 1874
chapters.kicker: PLEASURE ALSO BELONGS IN HIS BIOGRAPHY
paragraphs: At the beginning of 1874, Vincent told Theo that life in London was going well. He enjoyed his home, the city, and the people around him.
His letters leave room for a Vincent often overshadowed by later tragedy: curious, appreciative, and capable of taking pleasure in ordinary things.

views.label: January: Home and Art
views.title: January — A World Worth Looking At
paragraphs: In his January letter, Vincent moves between affection for his brother and enthusiasm for art. He lists painters he admires, praises Millet’s The Angelus, and encourages Theo to keep walking and loving nature.
For him, looking at the world and looking at pictures were connected. Painters could help people notice what they might otherwise overlook.
He also describes the satisfaction of having a comfortable home, alongside nature, art and poetry. Read this letter before the accounts of disappointment: happiness, too, belongs in his biography.

quote.attribution: Vincent to Theo · London, beginning of January 1874 · Letter 17

views.label: April: Gardens and Walks
views.title: April — A Garden and a Walk
paragraphs: By 30 April, Vincent was writing about flowering gardens and magnificent chestnut trees. He had sown sweet peas, poppies and mignonette, and was waiting to see what would grow.
He enjoyed walking between home and the office, a journey he estimated at about forty-five minutes. Yet pleasure in London coexisted with longing for Holland, especially Helvoirt.
These details need not become symbols of his future paintings. They matter first as the activities and attachments of a young man living away from home.

quote.text: He that sincerely loves nature, finds pleasure everywhere.
quote.attribution: Vincent to Theo · London, 30 April 1874 · Letter 22

chapters.prompt: What changes when we give his happiness as much attention as his suffering?

actions.label: Art Before Painting
actions.description: Optional branch · Follow a picture from Vincent to Theo

chapters.evidence: Dates and letter numbers follow the scholarly edition. The typeset quotations use the English version published by WebExhibits, which numbers these letters differently. The surrounding text is an independent summary, not part of the quotation.

chapters.title: An Uncertain Attachment
chapters.focus: What did this household mean to Vincent, and how did the relationship continue?
chapters.subtitle: A Home, a Hope, and a Departure
paragraphs: At Hackford Road, Vincent found a household he enjoyed. His family also became interested in the people with whom he was living.

A later family memoir places an unreturned attachment inside this happy period. Follow six moments: a familiar home, a family’s questions, an existing engagement, the remembered refusal, a summer with Anna and a later visit.

scenes.title: A Household He Enjoyed
scenes.subtitle: Rooms, a Garden, and Familiar Company
scenes.label: A BRIEF RETURN TO THE PREVIOUS CHAPTERS
paragraphs: The rooms and garden you have just encountered gave his London life a familiar setting. His letters describe pleasure in the house, attention to its flowers and the daily walk to work.
The family story of an attachment begins within that period of happiness—not in a place he described only through disappointment.
scenes.imageCaption: 87 Hackford Road, London · Photographed on 17 May 2016, not in 1873.
scenes.imageCredit: Photograph: Udimu / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Unmodified source image

actions.label: Return to A Life He Enjoyed

scenes.title: Questions Between Families
scenes.subtitle: How Close Had They Become?
scenes.label: FAMILY CORRESPONDENCE · JANUARY 1874
paragraphs: In a letter to Theo dated 6 January 1874, Anna passed on news of Vincent’s relationship with the household. According to the correspondence discussed in Elly Cassee’s research, Vincent had described himself and “Ursula” as being like a brother and sister. Anna nevertheless wondered whether their closeness might be love.
Here, a young man’s description and his sister’s curiosity do not quite coincide. The letter preserves the family wondering about an attachment; it does not establish a romance.
The name needs care. The house included Ursula Loyer and her daughter Eugénie. Later accounts have had to disentangle them.

record.label: EDITORIAL CORRESPONDENCE GUIDE · NOT AN ARCHIVE IMAGE
record.title: News Passed Between Siblings
record.body: Vincent writes to Anna; Anna passes his description and her own question on to Theo. This is a guide to the exchange discussed by Cassee, not a reconstruction of the letters.

actions.label: Read Anna’s Correspondence in Cassee’s Research

scenes.title: A Promise Already Made
scenes.subtitle: Eugénie’s Engagement
scenes.label: FAMILY CORRESPONDENCE · FEBRUARY 1874
paragraphs: On 24 February 1874, Anna wrote to Theo after receiving a letter from Vincent. He was in good spirits, enjoyed living with the Loyer family, and reported that Eugénie was engaged to a good-natured young man.

Eugénie’s engagement appears alongside his happiness in the household. This was a home whose other residents had commitments and possible futures of their own; her promise was already a subject of discussion in Vincent’s family.

record.label: PUBLISHED TRANSCRIPTION · NOT A MANUSCRIPT FACSIMILE
record.title: Anna to Theo
record.body: The linked transcription records Anna’s report of Vincent’s recent letter: he was in good spirits, enjoyed the household, and described Eugénie’s fiancé. Read the passage in its family context.

scenes.materialNote: The linked transcription is dated 24 February and addressed to Theo. It does not establish when Vincent declared his feelings; the engagement should not be introduced as something he certainly first discovered during an August confession.

scenes.title: The Story Jo Preserved
scenes.subtitle: A Declaration and a Refusal
scenes.label: LATER FAMILY ACCOUNT
paragraphs: In Jo van Gogh-Bonger’s later account, Vincent fell in love with the landlady’s daughter. When he declared his feelings, the young woman, whom Jo called Ursula, told him that she was already engaged to a former lodger.
Jo describes Vincent trying to persuade her to change her mind. He wanted her to break off the engagement, but his efforts failed.

She then follows him back to the Netherlands, where he appeared thinner, quieter and dejected. Affection had become a hope for a different life; in the story the family preserved, that hope was not returned.

record.label: RETROSPECTIVE MEMOIR · NOT AN EYEWITNESS TRANSCRIPT
record.title: Jo van Gogh-Bonger
record.body: The memoir supplies the declaration, refusal and disappointment. Its emotional sequence can be read as a story in its own right, alongside the correspondence.

scenes.materialNote: Jo identifies the woman as the daughter but calls her Ursula; she does not write that Vincent loved the mother. This is a later family memoir. His surviving letters from the period do not describe the declaration itself.

scenes.title: Summer with Anna
scenes.subtitle: Finding Work and Preparing to Move
scenes.label: LONDON · JULY–AUGUST 1874
paragraphs: By the end of July 1874, Anna was with Vincent in London. His letter of 31 July describes their walks and the search for a position for her. Reading, pictures and family responsibilities remained part of his daily life.

On 10 August, he told Theo that they were preparing to move. The new house was covered with ivy, identified by the letter editors as Ivy Cottage at 395 Kennington Road. He also wrote about their evening walks and promised to send another letter from the new address.
The letter records the practical shape of a departure: a sister beside him, another house to enter and a continuing exchange with Theo. It gives us more than a sudden escape after a refusal.
scenes.addressCaption: Preparing to move · Letter to Theo, 10 August 1874. The new address is identified by the letter editors; this is not a reconstruction of a journey.

scenes.title: Visiting Again
scenes.subtitle: The Household Remained in His Life
scenes.label: LONDON · NOVEMBER 1876
paragraphs: In a letter dated 25 November 1876, Vincent described another visit to Mrs Loyer in Clapham, shortly after her birthday. It was one stop on a long day walking through London and calling on people he knew.
The contact had not ended with his move from Hackford Road. This small later visit carries the relationship beyond the departure, without resolving the earlier attachment.

record.label: EDITORIAL LETTER SUMMARY · NOT A TRANSCRIPTION
record.title: Letter 99 · To Theo
record.body: This letter records a visit to Mrs Loyer shortly after her birthday. It does not say that Eugénie was present, or that the romantic disappointment had been resolved.

actions.label: How Vincent Later Remembered Young Love

comparison.title: Sources & Versions
comparison.subtitle: How the Attachment Has Been Understood

closing.title: Beyond Hackford Road
paragraphs: Vincent continued to seek a direction through work, reading and religious commitment. His early London letters already contained expressions of faith. Over the following years, teaching and religious work became part of his search for a useful life.
Follow the places, people and choices through which that search continued—not a single cause linking disappointment to religion.

chapters.title: Sources & Versions
chapters.subtitle: How Do We Know This Story?
paragraphs: A letter, a family memoir and a later interpretation do not speak from the same position.
This display separates what Vincent wrote, what others remembered, and what researchers have inferred. Different accounts remain visible without being treated as equally certain.

evidenceCards.title: Letters
evidenceCards.label: CONTEMPORARY CORRESPONDENCE
paragraphs: The letters displayed here describe a new room, a pleasant home, paintings, gardening and daily walks. They give us Vincent’s own account of these parts of his London life.
They do not narrate a romantic confession or rejection. Their silence cannot establish that nothing happened; equally, it does not allow us to supply the missing conversation.

evidenceCards.title: Family Recollections
evidenceCards.label: RETROSPECTIVE FAMILY ACCOUNT
paragraphs: Jo van Gogh-Bonger’s memoir presents disappointed love as a turning point. Her account links the episode with changes in Vincent’s behaviour and an increasingly religious life.
It preserves a family understanding of his experience. Yet it was written retrospectively, and its naming of the woman as Ursula has become part of the historical debate.
Read it as an influential account—not an eyewitness record of the encounter.

evidenceCards.title: Later Research
evidenceCards.label: LATER RESEARCH & INTERPRETATION
paragraphs: In 2019, Van Gogh specialist Martin Bailey revisited the story using census information and correspondence from Vincent’s sister Anna. He argues that Eugénie, rather than her mother, was the likely object of Vincent’s affection.
Bailey reports that Anna’s February 1874 correspondence already mentioned Eugénie’s engagement. This complicates a narrative in which Vincent first discovered it during a confession in August.

Eugénie married Samuel Plowman in 1878. Bailey considers him the likely earlier fiancé, but does not regard that identification as certain. This is a named specialist’s research article, not a peer-reviewed paper.

evidenceCards.title: Open Questions
evidenceCards.label: UNRESOLVED · CURATORIAL PERSPECTIVE
paragraphs: The accounts assembled here do not establish the exact words, date or circumstances of a confession, or fully explain Vincent’s departure.

Some narratives connect disappointed love with his turn towards religion. That connection is an interpretation, not a demonstrated psychological cause. Van Gogh House explicitly leaves the circumstances of his departure unresolved.
Uncertainty is not an invitation to invent a scene. It is a reason to leave space around the people involved.

chapters.prompt: Which details come from a document, which from memory, and which from interpretation?
chapters.evidence: The four cards distinguish evidence types; they are not a vote on which story is true. Full scans of Anna’s relevant letter and the census have not been verified here. No substitute archive pages have been invented.

chapters.title: Art Before Painting
chapters.subtitle: Learning to Look in the Art Trade
chapters.kicker: OPTIONAL BRANCH · NOT A LATER TURNING POINT
paragraphs: Before choosing art as a vocation, Vincent worked in the business of selling pictures.
His London correspondence discusses paintings, engravings and photographic reproductions. It also reveals a young man forming preferences and sharing them with his brother.

sections.title: Business and Enthusiasm
paragraphs: On 19 November 1873, Vincent wrote to Theo about their work for the same firm. He compared the demand for different reproductions, noted sales of engravings after Ingres, and discussed the success of photographs, especially coloured ones.
He also encouraged Theo to visit museums and read about art. Business and enthusiasm appear together: the letter does not present him as someone who had already rejected the art trade.
In April 1874, he mentioned sending Theo a photographic reproduction of Gustave Jean Jacquet’s Girl Holding a Sword. Published by Goupil & Cie, the photograph survives in Theo’s scrapbook.
Placed beside the letter, it offers a concrete example of a picture passing between the brothers. Consider it not as an early Van Gogh work, but as something he chose to share.

quote.text: You must write me sometime whom you like best among the older painters as well as among the moderns.
quote.attribution: Vincent to Theo · London, 19 November 1873 · Letter 15

chapters.prompt: Before asking what Vincent painted, ask what he chose to look at—and what he wanted someone else to see.
chapters.evidence: The reproduction is after Jacquet’s 1872 painting, not a Van Gogh painting or a portrait of Eugénie. This optional branch expands the working life introduced in A Life He Enjoyed; it is not a new chronological stage or a consequence of the attachment.

chapters.title: Turning to Faith
chapters.focus: How did teaching, study and preaching become possible directions?
chapters.subtitle: Reading, Teaching and a Possible Vocation
chapters.imageCaption: Vincent van Gogh, aged nineteen. Photograph by J. M. W. de Louw, The Hague, January 1873. This earlier portrait is not a photograph of his religious work in 1876.
chapters.imageCredit: J. M. W. de Louw · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain
paragraphs: After the art trade, Vincent explored teaching and religious work. In England in 1876, he worked in schools and became involved in preaching. His letter to Theo of 3 November describes his first sermon and includes its text.

Religion offered a possible direction, but the route was not straightforward. Further study and training preceded his move to the Belgian mining region. Read these changes as successive efforts to find a vocation, rather than as a single consequence of the London attachment.
chapters.prompt: What kind of work might give a life purpose?
chapters.evidence: An independent curatorial summary, grounded in the linked letters and institutional chronology. The portrait dates from January 1873; it is not evidence of an event in 1876. No single psychological cause is asserted.

chapters.title: Going Underground
chapters.focus: What were the miners facing, below ground and at home?
chapters.subtitle: What He Saw at Marcasse
chapters.imageCaption: Miners, Cuesmes. Catalogued as 1880 at the linked image source. This later drawing is not a photograph of Marcasse or a facsimile of the April 1879 letter. Open the letter to see its mine-work sketches.
chapters.imageCredit: Vincent van Gogh · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain
paragraphs: In April 1879, Vincent told Theo about spending six hours underground at Marcasse. He described descending about 700 metres, following narrow timber-supported passages and watching coal being cut by lamplight. Some miners stood; others worked lying flat. Children, both boys and girls, loaded coal into small wagons.

He drew the cramped working spaces in the letter. These small sketches make the account concrete: a body has to fit into the space left by the coal seam, and a narrow passage is also the way back out.

Above ground, the danger continued as illness and exhaustion. Vincent visited a miner recovering from severe burns. In another household, everyone had fever and almost no help. He recorded a woman’s observation about their situation:

quote.text: Here it is the sick who nurse the sick.
quote.attribution: A woman in a sick household, as reported by Vincent to Theo · April 1879 · Letter 151

chapters.title: Giving What He Had
chapters.focus: How did caring for others begin to endanger his own welfare?
chapters.subtitle: Care and His Own Living Conditions
chapters.imageCaption: Miners, Cuesmes. Catalogued as 1880 at the linked image source. A later drawing of working people, not an illustration documenting the nursing visits or Vincent’s hut in 1879.
chapters.imageCredit: Vincent van Gogh · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain
paragraphs: Vincent wanted to do more than speak about faith. He nursed injured people and kept watch with them at night. In February 1879, his father worried that this care was absorbing him completely, leaving too little strength for his other responsibilities.

Family correspondence describes him leaving the Denis household for a hut, without a bed or clean clothes. After an inspection, his mother reported a warning from local religious figures: if he refused their advice, he could lose his post. His father travelled to the Borinage to intervene.

In March, Vincent told Theo that the small house was now a workspace or study, and that he had agreed to board with the Denis family again. His commitment to helping others was real; so were the concerns about how he was living.

evidenceCards.title: A Later Family Account
evidenceCards.label: FAMILY MEMORY · WRITTEN AFTERWARDS
paragraphs: Jo van Gogh-Bonger later described him giving away money, clothes and his bed while trying to live by the teachings of Jesus. In her account, his intense devotion and self-neglect alarmed the religious authorities.

This is a retrospective family narrative, not the committee’s statement of its reasons. Read it beside the contemporary correspondence and the committee report, rather than treating all three as a single eyewitness account.

chapters.title: The Appointment Ends
chapters.focus: Why did sincere dedication not secure a lasting appointment?
chapters.subtitle: How the Committee Judged His Work
chapters.imageCaption: Miners, Cuesmes. Catalogued as 1880 at the linked image source. An artwork reproduction, not an image of the committee or its report.
chapters.imageCredit: Vincent van Gogh · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain
paragraphs: By August 1879, Vincent’s six-month trial as an evangelist had ended without renewal. He was given three months to look for another position. Caring so deeply for the people around him had not secured the vocation he had hoped for.

The committee’s 1879–1880 report contains both praise and criticism. It recognised his generosity towards sick and injured people, but judged that he lacked the speaking and organisational abilities needed to lead a congregation. It also noted that a meeting at Warquignies had lapsed during his appointment.

assessment.label: EDITORIAL SUMMARY · TWO ASPECTS OF THE SAME REPORT

items.title: What the Committee Praised
paragraphs: Care for the sick and injured, night watches, and the clothes and linen he gave away. It acknowledged devotion and self-sacrifice.

items.title: What the Committee Criticised
paragraphs: His suitability for preaching and leading congregational activity. It considered the results of the trial inadequate for continuing his employment.

chapters.title: Taking Up the Pencil
chapters.focus: After the appointment, how could he still be useful?
chapters.subtitle: Finding a Way to Be Useful
chapters.imageCaption: Miners, Cuesmes. Catalogued as 1880 at the linked image source. A drawing of working people, shown here alongside his letters about finding a direction through drawing.
chapters.imageCredit: Vincent van Gogh · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain
paragraphs: Losing the appointment did not instantly turn Vincent into an artist. In August 1879, he was already filling sketchbooks and drawing at night. His direction remained unsettled, and the months ahead brought estrangement and discouragement.
In a letter dated approximately 22–24 June 1880, he asked how he could contribute to the world. The question was larger than the position he had lost.

By September, he described renewed effort in drawing: working through Bargue’s course and studying anatomy and perspective. He also wrote of his fellow-feeling for miners and weavers, hoping to bring their often-unnoticed lives into view.

The wish to help did not vanish when his religious employment ended. Drawing was becoming another way to attend to people, but it required learning and sustained work. The next chapter follows that practice.

quote.text: what could I be good for, couldn’t I serve and be useful in some way
quote.attribution: Vincent to Theo · Cuesmes, approximately 22–24 June 1880 · Letter 155

actions.label: Read the Letter about Being Useful

chapters.title: Sources & Versions
chapters.subtitle: Why Was He Not Retained?
paragraphs: Practical care, personal living conditions and the expectations of an evangelist’s work appear differently in these records. None needs to be hidden for the story to remain moving.
Read the three accounts together. Consider what each records directly, what it judges, and when it was written.

evidenceCards.title: Contemporary Correspondence
evidenceCards.label: VINCENT AND HIS FAMILY · 1878–1880
paragraphs: Vincent’s letters describe Bible readings, visits to the sick, the descent at Marcasse and the daily lives around him. Family letters quoted in the scholarly edition record concern about nursing, housing, clothing and refusal to accept advice.
The warning from local religious figures and his father’s intervention concern his conduct and welfare. These records do not reduce the later non-renewal to a single cause.

evidenceCards.title: The Committee’s Account
evidenceCards.label: REPORT FOR 1879–1880 · EXTRACT IN LETTER 153, NOTE 4
paragraphs: The report explicitly recognises care and self-sacrifice. Its explanation for not retaining him centres on the demands of preaching and congregational leadership, including the lapsed Warquignies meeting.

The appointment document cited in Letter 149 dates the six-month post from 1 February 1879; the committee had discussed him on 14 January. The report is a later institutional assessment, not a transcript of a dismissal conversation.

evidenceCards.title: A Later Family Narrative
evidenceCards.label: JO VAN GOGH-BONGER · RETROSPECTIVE MEMOIR
paragraphs: Jo’s account places greater emphasis on giving possessions away, intense religious practice and self-neglect. It helps explain the familiar portrayal of a man whose attempt to share poverty unsettled his employers.
That emphasis belongs to her later narrative. The suggestion that he embarrassed the church is not presented here as the committee’s documented wording or its sole stated reason.

chapters.evidence: The 1880 Miners reproduction provides a visual connection with working people, not photographic evidence of the 1879 episodes. The original mine-work sketches can be opened from Letter 151 at the scholarly edition. No manuscript image, historical interior or dismissal scene has been invented.

chapters.title: Finding a Way Forward
chapters.focus: How could an interest in art become useful, sustainable work?
chapters.subtitle: Returning to the Pencil
paragraphs: The end of religious employment had not supplied a new profession. By 1880, Vincent still needed a livelihood and a way to contribute. Art was already familiar to him; deciding to work at it meant finding something he could actually do each day.

In September he told Theo about an earlier journey to Courrières, where he hoped to approach Jules Breton. He reached the painter’s studio but did not introduce himself. Fields, cottages and working people remained vivid in his account, alongside exhaustion and poverty.

Back in Cuesmes, drawing gave that attention a task. He borrowed prints, studied books and asked Theo for help. Renewed energy did not remove his shortage of money or a suitable working room. It made another attempt possible: a sheet, a model to copy, and a day spent learning.
chapters.prompt: What would it take to turn something you care about into a daily practice?
chapters.evidence: Letter 158 recalls the journey retrospectively; its date is not the date of the journey. This is a gradual change of direction, not an invented scene of sudden conversion from preacher to painter.

actions.label: Before the Decision · Learning to Look
actions.description: Optional look back to London · art and nature before 1880

chapters.title: A Teacher on Paper
chapters.focus: What did repeated exercises teach his eye and hand?
chapters.subtitle: Exercises, Repetition and the Hand
paragraphs: A printed lesson could be returned to as often as necessary. Charles Bargue’s drawing course, published by Goupil, supplied models derived from plaster casts and master drawings. The trade in reproductions Vincent had known as an employee became part of his training.

On 7 September 1880 he reported finishing sixty sheets of Bargue’s charcoal exercises, lent by Hermanus Tersteeg. He had worked for about a fortnight, from early morning until evening. In January 1881 he was copying the complete exercises for a third time.

Repetition was meant to change what he could see. When he returned to living models in Etten, he credited those exercises with helping him measure, notice proportions and grasp the broad outlines. Copying was a preparation for looking, not the final destination.
chapters.prompt: Look at an outline before its details. Where does the weight of the form sit?
chapters.evidence: The lesson sequence is an editorial guide based on his letters, not an image of a surviving exercise sheet. The sixty-sheet report and the third repetition belong to different letters and dates.

chapters.title: Learning from Millet
chapters.focus: Why did figures at work become both subjects and lessons?
chapters.subtitle: Bodies at Work
paragraphs: In August, Vincent asked Theo to lend him reproductions of Jean-François Millet’s Labours of the Fields. He wanted examples of diggers and a winnower, and had already copied The Four Times of the Day and The Sower. He asked for loans, not specially purchased pictures.

By September he had drawn The Sower five times: twice small, three times large. The figure continued to occupy him. A person’s balance, the reach of an arm and the effort of a bent body gave him something specific to work out on paper.

Millet offered a meeting point between Vincent’s attention to labouring people and his need to learn figure drawing. That connection is a curatorial reading of his choices, not a quotation or proof of a single motive. Theo’s help and the circulation of printed images made those choices practicable.
chapters.prompt: Follow the gesture rather than the face. How does a body show its work?
chapters.evidence: The 1880 copies described in the letters are not automatically the surviving early Sower dated April 1881. The scholarly notes also leave the precise reproduction used in August 1880 uncertain.

chapters.title: Seeking Other Artists
chapters.focus: Who supplied advice, examples and a place to work?
chapters.subtitle: Guidance in Brussels
paragraphs: In Brussels, Willem Roelofs advised Vincent to draw directly from plaster casts or a living model, with guidance. Studying printed examples was not enough. Proportion, anatomy, light and shade, and perspective had to be brought to the things in front of him.

Vincent also worked at Anthon van Rappard’s studio. In April 1881 he described the problem of losing that workspace: his own bedroom was too small and poorly lit. He hoped to live where he could meet other painters and receive practical advice.

He imagined a craft that might earn a living. In January he discussed drawing working people for magazine or book illustration, and the need to afford models. Literature and pictures of ordinary lives belonged to that ambition. He worked largely through his own efforts, but not without other people.
chapters.prompt: Choose a person in the support network. What made their help different?
chapters.evidence: Academy registration is documented. The scholarly edition also cites participation in a December 1880 competition; see Sources & Versions for the limits of reconstructing his classroom experience. Neither wholly isolated self-teaching nor prolonged academic training is assumed.

chapters.title: Drawing the Life Around Him
chapters.focus: How did printed lessons become studies of real people?
chapters.subtitle: Models in Etten
paragraphs: In Etten, advice from Anton Mauve helped Vincent return to living models. One was the labourer Piet Kaufmann. Getting someone to pose meant negotiation, time and money; observation depended on another person’s cooperation.

His September letter lists a man with a spade drawn five times in different poses, two sowers and two studies of a girl with a broom. A woman peeling potatoes and an old man by the fire also became subjects. These were repeated attempts to understand familiar actions, not a single finished image of rural life.

Bargue’s lessons now had a practical test. He could measure a figure and establish its broad shape, then try again when the proportions did not work. Labourers and household tasks supplied both the world he wanted to notice and the forms he needed to learn.
chapters.prompt: Choose one everyday action. What changes when it is seen from another pose?
chapters.evidence: Letter 172 contains small sketches and a description of the studies. Open those sketches in the original edition; a letter sketch, a named study and a surviving independent drawing are different kinds of object.

chapters.title: Nature and Reality
chapters.focus: What did working from life require beyond a love of scenery?
chapters.subtitle: A Familiar World to Study
chapters.imageCaption: Road in Etten, 1881. Chalk, pencil, pastel and watercolour; underdrawing in pen and brown ink. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, 1975.1.774.
chapters.imageCredit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Open Access / CC0 · 459193
paragraphs: When the weather allowed, he went out to draw. In May he described huts, barns, trees and woodcutters, as well as carts, ploughs, harrows and wheelbarrows. Landscape and working life were not separate worlds in these observations.

In July, heat could send him indoors to copy Holbein. He experimented with textured Ingres paper and a reed pen. In October he described about seven large studies of pollard-willow trunks along the road to the station and Leur. Attention became a routine shaped by weather, materials and repeated encounters.

Road in Etten brings several of those concerns into view: a receding road, trees and a worker carrying a broom. Follow the road into the distance, then return to the figure and the marks that hold the scene together. The picture is an independent work, not a facsimile of the road sketch in his October letter.

In November he wrote passionately to Van Rappard about nature and reality. His argument expresses an artistic commitment to lived experience; it is not a neutral verdict on every kind of academy teaching. Here, loving nature means staying with something long enough to observe and attempt it.
chapters.prompt: Follow the road, compare the trunks, and find the figure. What makes this a studied place?
chapters.evidence: Working ‘from nature’ could also mean observing objects, casts or live models. This work’s mixed materials and date follow the Met record. No direct identity with Letter 174’s sketch, or unproved influence from another artist, is asserted.

chapters.title: Taking Up the Brush
chapters.focus: How did guidance turn drawing practice towards painting?
chapters.subtitle: Lessons with Mauve
paragraphs: At the beginning of December, Mauve put Vincent in front of a still life of old wooden clogs and other objects. He also went to Mauve in the evenings to draw. Painting began with ordinary things and practical instruction, not a sudden release from the need to learn.

Later that month he discussed painted studies and watercolours, and a technical problem: Mauve thought he was working too close to his model. Without enough distance, judging proportions was difficult. A larger room, rent and the conditions of work were part of the next lesson.

The early works bring us close to that labour of learning. Open a drawing to explore its materials, its setting and the evidence behind its story. Road in Etten remains in Hall 01’s Early Works; the drawings, paintings and lives of The Hague continue in Hall 02 · Earth and Labour.
chapters.prompt: What do the next works reveal about a skill still being built?
chapters.evidence: Letters 191 and 193 describe the instruction and its difficulties. No unverified still life is substituted for the objects named in the letter. The detailed Hague biography belongs to the next hall.

chapters.title: Before the Decision
chapters.subtitle: Learning to Look
paragraphs: Choosing art as work in 1880 did not mean discovering pictures for the first time. Years earlier, Vincent discussed Millet, Breton, Corot, Rousseau and Dutch painters with Theo. Walking, reading and looking at art were already connected in his everyday life.

This short return to the January 1874 letter offers a starting point for the later practice. The full account of the house, garden and London work remains in A Life He Enjoyed rather than being repeated here.

quote.text: Painters understand nature and love it, and teach us to see.
quote.attribution: Vincent to Theo · Beginning of January 1874 · Letter 17

chapters.evidence: A brief excerpt from the scholarly translation, not a manuscript image. This earlier interest is not evidence that he had already chosen an artistic career in 1874.

chapters.title: Sources & Versions
chapters.subtitle: How We Know about the First Years of Learning
paragraphs: Letters describe intentions, requests and difficulties at particular moments. Printed models, letter sketches and independent works must be identified separately. Open a question below, then return to the same place in the story.

evidenceCards.title: When Did He Become an Artist?
evidenceCards.label: INTEREST · DIRECTION · CONTINUING PRACTICE
paragraphs: Early interest in art, the decision to pursue it as work around 1880, and developing a workable practice are not the same event. The letters show plans changing, help being sought and the problem of earning a living. A surviving study does not date an artist’s ‘birth’ to a single day.

evidenceCards.title: What Does ‘From Nature’ Mean?
evidenceCards.label: DIRECT OBSERVATION · NOT ONLY LANDSCAPE
paragraphs: In Letter 160, Roelofs’s advice explicitly includes casts and a living model. Outdoor landscape is one application of direct observation, not its whole meaning. The Etten letters also describe work tools, people, weather and the choice to continue indoors.

evidenceCards.title: Was He Self-Taught?
evidenceCards.label: EXERCISES · ADVICE · ACADEMY RECORDS
paragraphs: Much of the work was self-directed, but books, borrowed prints, artists’ advice and shared workspaces mattered. The support network is a guide to specific help, not a claim that every person taught the same lesson.

Letter 160’s current scholarly note 3 records Brussels academy enrolment in the first week of November 1880. It discusses older doubts about attendance, then cites research on his participation in a competition on 5 December. Registration and that competition should not be erased; they also do not establish prolonged or comprehensive classroom training.

evidenceCards.title: Which Early Drawings Survive?
evidenceCards.label: A LETTER IS NOT AN OBJECT IDENTIFICATION
paragraphs: Some early copies are lost; others cannot securely be matched to an individual mention. Letter 156’s notes date the known early Sower to April 1881, rather than the August 1880 request. Small sketches inside letters are distinct from separately catalogued works.

Road in Etten is shown with its Met catalogue date and materials. It is not labelled as the exact drawing attached to Letter 174. The Bargue lesson guide and the support network are present-day editorial aids, clearly distinguished from historical images.

chapters.evidence: Dates and letter numbers follow the scholarly edition. Original manuscript views and full translations are accessed at their source; the exhibit does not generate substitute archive pages or imply permission for wholesale reproduction.

chapters.title: Sources & Versions
chapters.subtitle: How the Attachment Has Been Understood
paragraphs: These accounts do more than disagree about names. They give the episode different shapes: a family’s remembered refusal, a revised identification, a different explanation of disappointment, and a cautious history of the house.
Open an account to see what it actually contributes. The letters remain available below; the date, author and kind of source matter alongside the story.

evidenceCards.title: The Family Memoir
evidenceCards.label: JO VAN GOGH-BONGER · RETROSPECTIVE FAMILY ACCOUNT
paragraphs: Jo preserves the declaration, refusal and disappointment that give the episode its familiar narrative. She describes the landlady’s daughter but calls her Ursula.
She assembled the account retrospectively from family material and information received from Theo. It supplies a remembered scene, not an eyewitness transcript or a secure date for the declaration.

evidenceCards.title: A Revised Identification
evidenceCards.label: MARTIN BAILEY · LATER SPECIALIST RESEARCH
paragraphs: Bailey revisits the identity through Anna’s correspondence and family records. He identifies Eugénie as the likely subject of the attachment and considers Samuel Plowman, whom she married in 1878, a possible earlier fiancé.
His article reproduces later photographs of Eugénie and Samuel in a family locket. It is not a portrait of Vincent with Eugénie, or an image of the declaration.

The linked family-letter transcription is dated 24 February 1874 and addressed to Theo. It mentions Eugénie’s engagement. The date belongs to this published transcription; it does not establish when Vincent declared his feelings.

evidenceCards.title: A Different Scholarly Reading
evidenceCards.label: ELLY CASSEE · VAN GOGH MUSEUM JOURNAL, 1996
paragraphs: In her museum-journal article In love: Vincent van Gogh’s first true love, Cassee questions the weight later biography has given to the London romance. She examines Anna’s correspondence and Vincent’s earlier attachment to his cousin Caroline Haanebeek.

She proposes that disappointment involving Caroline may help explain the unhappiness associated with this period. This is an alternative scholarly reading, not proof that the London attachment never happened.

evidenceCards.title: A Cautious Institutional Account
evidenceCards.label: VAN GOGH HOUSE LONDON · HERITAGE INSTITUTION
paragraphs: Van Gogh House describes affection for Eugénie as rumoured and leaves the circumstances of his departure unresolved.
The account places the relationship within the life of the house without allowing a familiar love story to explain every later choice.

chapters.evidence: These are independent synopses, not reproduced manuscript pages. The family transcription and Cassee’s article are readable sources; the locket is viewed on Bailey’s site with its original credit. No substitute archive images or portraits have been invented.

chapters.title: Remembering an Earlier Love
chapters.subtitle: A Letter Written in 1881
chapters.kicker: A LATER REFLECTION · THE GIRL IS NOT NAMED
paragraphs: In November 1881, while discussing his feelings for Kee Vos, Vincent reflected on an earlier attachment. He recalled giving up on a girl who married someone else, and the long sorrow that followed.
He also questioned the way he had approached love when he was younger. It is his own later reflection on an early disappointment, but it is not a dated account of the London declaration.
He did not name the girl. This passage should not be labelled as a recollection of Eugénie: its precise identification remains open.
chapters.evidence: Cassee discusses this passage in her 1996 museum-journal article, including the possibility that the earlier attachment concerned Caroline Haanebeek. The reading here is an independent summary, not a reproduced translation.

materials.caption: Choose a name to separate household ties from later interpretations.

people.name: Vincent van Gogh
people.body: Vincent rented a room here while working in London. His surviving letters describe the lodgings and his daily life; they do not recount a confession of love.

people.name: Sarah Ursula Loyer
people.body: The widowed Mrs Loyer let rooms and helped run a boys’ school. Jo van Gogh-Bonger’s later memoir called the woman in the love story Ursula; later research questions that identification.

people.name: Eugénie Loyer
people.body: Bailey argues that Eugénie was the likely object of Vincent’s affection. Van Gogh House describes the attachment as rumoured. Neither wording establishes a documented romantic relationship.

people.name: Samuel Plowman
people.body: Eugénie married Samuel in 1878. Bailey considers him the likely earlier fiancé mentioned in the family story, but explicitly leaves that identification uncertain.

events.label: Contemporary letters
events.body: Lodgings, art, gardening and daily life—not an account of a romantic confession.

events.label: Reported correspondence
events.body: Bailey reports that Anna’s correspondence already mentions Eugénie’s engagement. The original letter is not displayed here.

events.label: Later marriage
events.body: Eugénie marries Samuel Plowman. This does not settle the earlier fiancé’s identity.

materials.title: The Household Behind the Story
materials.caption: A working household, not only the setting of a love story.

sections.title: Letting Rooms
sections.body: For the widowed Sarah Ursula Loyer, taking in lodgers was part of earning a living.

sections.title: A Boys’ School
sections.body: Vincent’s September 1873 letter mentions the boys’ school in the household. Domestic life and teaching occupied the same address.

sections.title: Traces of Everyday Business
sections.body: Restoration brought insurance papers bearing Ursula’s signature to light. They are evidence of household administration, not proof of the love story.

materials.title: When an Attribution Changes
materials.caption: The Hackford Road drawing was once attributed to Vincent. Martin Bailey’s 2023 account reports that the Van Gogh Museum rejected the attribution and presents the drawing as anonymous.
materials.credit: Martin Bailey · The Art Newspaper · 1 September 2023
materials.rights: Research reference only. The drawing is not installed as a confirmed Van Gogh work.

materials.kind: A PICTURE VINCENT SENT TO THEO
materials.caption: Photographic reproduction after Gustave Jean Jacquet’s painting of 1872. Published by Goupil & Cie; preserved in Theo van Gogh’s scrapbook. Vincent mentioned sending it on 30 April 1874. It is not a portrait of Eugénie Loyer.

materials.rights: View the actual reproduction in the original edition’s image viewer. No substitute painting or fabricated archive image is used.

materials.title: A Journey Recalled, a Task Begun
materials.caption: Read the journey as Vincent remembered it, not as a scene of sudden revelation.

sections.title: The earlier journey
sections.body: Vincent recalled walking to Courrières, reaching Jules Breton’s studio and leaving without introducing himself. The letter’s date is not the date of the journey.

sections.title: The work now at hand
sections.body: Books, borrowed prints and drawing offered something practical to return to. Limited space and money remained part of that work.

materials.credit: Original gallery reading aid · Based on Letters 156 and 158
materials.rights: Editorial summary, not a letter transcription, travel map or reconstructed historical scene. The manuscript and complete translation are available at the original edition.

materials.title: A Programme to Repeat
materials.caption: An editorial guide to his practice—not a reproduction of a Bargue plate.

sections.title: Begin with the outline
sections.body: Printed models gave him forms to compare: broad outlines, relationships between parts, and the placement of light and shade.

sections.title: Work through the sheets
sections.body: On 7 September 1880, he reported completing sixty Bargue charcoal sheets in a fortnight, working from morning until evening.

sections.title: Return and compare
sections.body: By January 1881 he described a third complete repetition. A course on paper could be revisited while he sought guidance and practised other subjects.

materials.credit: Original gallery study guide · Based on Letters 136, 157, 160 and 162
materials.rights: Original explanatory guide, not an archival teaching sheet. The course description and illustrated example can be checked in Letter 136, note 22; no unverified plate or supposed matching Vincent copy is displayed.

materials.title: From a Printed Example to a Working Figure
materials.caption: Keep the artist he studied separate from the drawings he was trying to make.

sections.title: Study Source · Millet
sections.body: The requested reproductions included The Labours of the Fields, diggers and a winnower. These were examples to borrow and study, not pictures painted by Vincent.

sections.title: Vincent’s Work · Learning the Figure
sections.body: He reported making copies and trying to improve the figures in a drawing of miners going to the pit. Five repetitions of The Sower are mentioned in September 1880. A surviving Sower from April 1881 must not be passed off as one of those earlier copies.

materials.credit: Original gallery comparison guide · Letter 156 and its work-identification notes; Letter 157
materials.rights: Textual study comparison, not a pair of identified matching artworks. Consult the edition’s illustrations and object notes for the actual reproductions and surviving works.

materials.title: The Help Behind the Practice
materials.caption: Choose a person to see what their help made possible at this stage.

people.name: Theo van Gogh
people.body: Vincent asked Theo to lend Millet reproductions rather than buy new ones. Later he asked him to bring textured Ingres paper suitable for pen work. Their letters connect encouragement to particular things he needed to keep practising.

people.name: Hermanus Tersteeg
people.body: The former Goupil colleague in The Hague was asked to lend the drawing examples. Borrowing the course made an organised programme of exercises available without requiring Vincent to purchase the whole set.

people.name: Willem Roelofs
people.body: In Brussels, Roelofs urged direct work from casts or living models, with help from an experienced artist. The advice challenged Vincent to move beyond copying flat examples alone.

people.name: Anthon van Rappard
people.body: Vincent’s April 1881 letter describes working in Van Rappard’s studio and benefiting from the contact. He still needed room, company and guidance as he worked towards earning a living.

people.name: Anton Mauve
people.body: Mauve encouraged work with living models, then gave him practical painting lessons in The Hague. His advice about working farther from the model brought space and judging proportions into the learning process.

materials.credit: Original gallery contact guide · Independent summaries of the linked correspondence
materials.rights: Editorial guide to documented assistance, not an archival relationship chart. No invented portraits, dialogue or studio photographs are used.

actions.label: Read about Roelofs and the Academy

materials.title: A Body in More Than One Position
materials.caption: The original letter includes small sketches. Open the edition to examine the actual marks.

sections.title: Return to the same model
sections.body: Piet Kaufmann posed with a spade. Vincent reported five positions of a digger, studying how a familiar action changed the arrangement of the body.

sections.title: Look at ordinary tasks
sections.body: Sowing, sweeping, peeling potatoes and sitting beside a fire supplied other poses. These were people who cooperated with him, not only subjects observed from a distance.

sections.title: Make the work possible
sections.body: He paid the models. Finding someone willing to pose, making time and meeting the expense belonged to the practice as much as pencil and paper.

materials.credit: Original gallery pose guide · Based on Letter 172
materials.rights: Editorial reading aid. No invented pose drawing or substitute manuscript is shown; the actual letter sketches remain available through the scholarly edition.

materials.title: Paper, Weather and a Place to Work
materials.caption: Tools and circumstances shaped what could be studied on a particular day.

sections.title: Outside when possible
sections.body: In May he described drawing buildings, trees, woodcutters and agricultural tools outdoors whenever the weather allowed.

sections.title: A paper suited to the pen
sections.body: In July he requested textured Ingres paper for pen work, especially the reed pen. Local alternatives could be too smooth or too expensive.

sections.title: Change the work, keep practising
sections.body: When the heath was too hot for outdoor drawing, he copied a Holbein example indoors. In autumn he returned repeatedly to the willow trunks beside a familiar road.

materials.credit: Original gallery materials guide · Based on Letters 167, 169 and 174
materials.rights: Editorial summary, not a display of Vincent’s original drawing tools or paper. Road in Etten is shown separately with its museum image credit and object record.

actions.label: Open Road in Etten’s Museum Record

materials.title: Objects, Distance and Proportion
materials.caption: Painting introduced another set of practical problems—not an instant transformation into the artist we know.

sections.title: A still life to begin
sections.body: Mauve put old wooden clogs and other objects before him to paint. Vincent also visited in the evenings to draw.

sections.title: Step farther back
sections.body: After returning to Etten, he recalled advice to work farther from the model. More space would help him judge proportions; finding a suitable room therefore mattered.

topics.title: Among the Miners
topics.subtitle: A Calling in the Borinage
topics.summary: Dangerous work, practical care, an appointment that ended, and the search for another way to be useful.

introduction.title: Faith, Care and the End of an Appointment
paragraphs: Vincent arrived in the Borinage hoping to find a lasting place in religious work. In December 1878, he described miners returning through the snow and the small homes around the pits. He held Bible readings, visited the sick and wanted to stay.

His six-month appointment began on 1 February 1879. Caring for injured and sick people became absorbing work. As he gave more of himself, his family grew alarmed by his living conditions, and local religious authorities pressed him to accept advice.

He was not retained. The committee acknowledged generosity and sacrifice but judged his preaching and congregational work inadequate. His future remained unsettled; the wish to be useful did not disappear.

topics.title: Learning to Draw
topics.subtitle: A Direction Taking Shape
topics.summary: Borrowed models, advice and repeated observation turn a possible future into daily work.

introduction.title: A Possible Future, Made into Daily Work
paragraphs: By 1880, Vincent was looking for sustainable work and a way to contribute. Theo encouraged his artistic direction, and drawing began to occupy more of his days.

Borrowed prints, exercises, books and contact with artists gave that direction a practical shape. In Etten, outdoor work and repeated studies of local people brought the lessons to life: materials, proportion, and the next attempt.

Follow the subjects and methods of these first years, or go straight to the Early Works. The London look back is optional; the main story moves from finding a direction to building a practice and working from life.
